cards.back: Where a signal starts, what it passes through, and where it ends up. When something’s wrong, follow it one stage at a time.
Which device and channels audio comes in on and goes out through. In a DAW, choose the device in the audio settings, then the input on each track.
Enables a track to record. Arm the track you mean to record onto, and only that one.
The preamp level at the start of a channel. Set it first to get a healthy signal, then use faders to balance the mix.
Get a healthy level with input gain first. Faders balance a mix; they can’t rescue a weak or distorted input.
0 dBFS is the digital ceiling. A signal that hits it clips and distorts, and turning it down later won’t undo that. Leave headroom.
Too loud clips. Too quiet buries the sound in noise. Just right: peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS.
One audio channel. One mic into one input is a mono source.
Two audio channels, usually left and right. A stereo mic pair is panned one left, one right.
Meters can’t tell you about distortion, noise, or the wrong mic. Record a short test and listen back before the real take.

Power sent to a mic through its cable. Condenser mics always need it. Dynamic mics don’t care whether it’s on or off. Ribbon mics must never get it. (Rare exceptions exist, like tube mics with their own power supply.)
Sensitive and detailed. Needs 48V phantom power. A common choice for acoustic instruments and ensembles.
Rugged and handles loud sources well. Doesn’t need phantom power. A common choice for live vocals and amps.
Smooth-sounding and fragile, usually with a figure-8 pickup. Keep phantom power off (rare exception: some modern active ribbons need it).
Gets mics and instruments into the computer and audio back out. Inside: preamps to raise mic level, and converters.
A/D turns the voltage from a mic or instrument into numbers the computer can record. D/A turns it back into voltage for speakers or headphones.
Three-pin, locking, balanced connector. The standard cable for microphones.
TS (tip-sleeve, one black ring): unbalanced, like a guitar cable. TRS (tip-ring-sleeve, two rings): balanced line signals, or stereo headphones.
The small headphone-size plug on phones and laptops. Usually stereo.
An input that takes either an XLR plug or a ¼″ plug. Common on audio interfaces.
Mute silences a track. Solo plays only that track (and any other soloed tracks). Pan places it between left and right.
Creates a finished audio file from your session, such as a WAV you can hand in or send.
The project (session) is your editable working file. The deliverable is the finished export someone else receives. Keep both.
Before you record, know which folder or drive your project and audio files go to, and name things so you can find them later.
Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO/gain together set how bright the image is. Change one and you may need to adjust another.
You set aperture, shutter, and gain yourself, so the brightness doesn’t drift on its own when the lighting or the shot changes.
The lens opening that controls how much light gets in. A higher f-number means a smaller opening and less light.
How long each frame is exposed. It affects brightness and how motion looks: slower shutter, more motion blur.
Brightens the image electronically. The tradeoff is more noise, or grain.
How many frames are recorded each second, such as 24, 30, or 60 fps. Choose it on purpose before you record.
A common starting point is a shutter about twice the frame rate: 1/60 at 30 fps, 1/50 at 24 fps.
Tells the camera what white looks like under the current light, so colors look right. It’s set in Kelvin; the Cameras activity used 3200 K.
Autofocus lets the camera choose what’s sharp, and it can hunt. Manual focus stays where you set it, which is safer for a fixed recital shot.
What’s in the shot and where it sits. Leave sensible room around the performers and keep the frame steady and level.
Record a few seconds, then check focus, exposure, color, and sound, and confirm the file is really on the card.
Source → mic, DI, or playback → mixer → amplifier (if needed) → speakers.
Converts an instrument or line signal, like a keyboard, into a balanced mic-level signal for the run to the mixer.
The audience mix: what the room hears.
The performer mix: what musicians hear on stage. It can be different from the mains.
Active (powered) speakers have an amplifier built in. Passive speakers need an external power amplifier.
A howl or squeal when sound from a speaker gets back into a mic and loops. Lower the level, and keep mics behind the speakers and aimed away.
Speakers ON last. Speakers OFF first. That keeps pops and thumps from upstream gear out of the speakers.
Before turning anything up, know what feeds the mains, the monitors, and the recording.
Test every important input, output, and playback source before the audience arrives, not during the first song.
Two directional mics with their capsules together, angled apart (often 90°). Very mono-compatible.
Two mics spaced apart, often omnis. A wide, spacious image, but it can have phase problems when summed to mono.
Two cardioid mics about 17 cm apart, angled 110°. A near-coincident middle ground between XY and A/B.
Pan one mic hard left and the other hard right. Both panned center collapses the stereo image.
Set both channels of a stereo pair to the same input gain, so the image isn’t pulled toward one side.
Be ready on time, communicate early, stay engaged, take care of gear, help your group, and finish the whole job.
If the call is 7:00, you’re set up and ready to work at 7:00, not just walking in.
Stereo audio capture · Video recording · Basic live sound · Data management & archiving · Post production.
A separate mix path. On the X32, buses feed things like Monitor 1 and Monitor 2, independent of Main L/R.
The overall level of a bus, such as one monitor mix, separate from each channel’s send into it.
Turns the faders into send levels for one selected bus, so you can build that monitor mix with the faders.
The mic or bodypack transmits to a paired receiver, and the receiver’s output goes to a mixer input. Check it’s paired and showing signal.
Carries many channels of audio over a standard computer network instead of separate audio cables.
Transmit channels send audio onto the network. Receive channels pick it up.
The routing software. Click where a transmitter channel meets a receiver channel to make a route (a subscription).
Lets a computer send and receive Dante channels, so a DAW can use the network as its audio I/O.
Records a phrase and plays it back on repeat so you can play over it. In our rig, that’s the Boss RC-30.
Live: guitar or uke → Zoom G3X → B205D Channel 3. Loop: G3X balanced out → RC-30 → B205D Channel 2.
Bring up the headset vocal channel last because it’s the most feedback-prone, and lower it first if feedback starts.
Keep each adapter with its own device. The RC-30 and MicroKorg both use 9V adapters with opposite polarity, so never swap them.
The very small signal from a microphone. It needs a preamp to bring it up.
The signal from a pickup or other high-impedance source, such as an electric guitar. A DI box helps connect it to a mixer.
The usual mixer-to-powered-device signal. A mixer’s main and aux outputs are line level.
The power-amplified signal that a passive speaker needs. It comes from a power amp, not from a mixer’s output.
Brings a small source, like a microphone, up to a usable level. It is the early stage of the channel.
Creates the speaker-driving power. It takes a line-level signal in and puts speaker level out.
Never connect a mixer line output directly to a passive loudspeaker. A power amp goes between them.
Needs AC power and a line input. The power amp lives in the cabinet.

cards.front: On an unfamiliar mixer, find first…
cards.back: A mic input, a line/stereo input, a main output, and a monitoring output.
Gain happens early. EQ, aux sends, pan, mute, and the fader come along the path after it.
XLR inputs feed the microphone preamps. ¼-inch and stereo line inputs take other source types.
Main, aux, control-room, phones, and record outputs each do a different job. Know what feeds what before you raise levels.
A channel can feed Main L/R (the audience), an aux or monitor mix (a performer), headphones or control room (the engineer), and a recording or streaming feed.
Usually feeds the audience system. It answers: what should the audience hear?
A bus is an internal mix path. An output connector is where that path physically leaves the mixer.
Channel → aux send → aux bus → aux output → monitor. The aux output is still line level, so a passive monitor needs a power amp first.
Takes some of a channel and sends it to another mix. Each channel can send a different amount.
Answers: what does this performer need to hear? It doesn’t have to match the audience mix.

cards.front: “More of me” vs. “everything is too quiet”
cards.back: “More of my voice”: raise that channel’s aux send. “My whole monitor is too quiet”: raise the aux master or output level.
Taps the channel before the fader, so the send doesn’t change when front-of-house moves the fader. Useful for performer monitors.
Follows the channel fader. Useful for effects and some recording or streaming situations.
Don’t assume every aux is configured the same way. Check the mixer.

cards.front: Vocal too loud in the house
cards.back: If the singer’s monitor send is pre-fader, lowering the vocal in Main L/R leaves their monitor about the same. That’s one reason monitor mixes use pre-fader sends.
PFL is pre-fader listen and AFL is after-fader listen. Different mixers use different labels for the same idea.
Listen to or meter a signal without necessarily sending it to the audience. Use it for setup and troubleshooting before turning up the room.
A locking speaker-level connector between a power amp and a passive speaker.
A common consumer unbalanced stereo connection.

cards.front: A connector doesn’t define the signal
cards.back: XLR and ¼-inch connections can carry different signals depending on the situation. The connector is a clue, not an answer.
Used for wall power. In the United States, about 120V AC at 60 Hz.
What batteries provide. Many pieces of audio equipment run on DC.
Often converts AC from the wall into the DC a device needs.
Carries the electrical power.
Provides the normal return path.
A safety connection that helps protect people if something goes wrong.
Never remove or defeat the ground pin to solve an audio problem.
Just because a power adapter fits physically does not mean it is safe. Check before you plug in.
AC or DC? Voltage matches? Polarity matches? Enough amperage? Connector actually fits?
Must match. A device that requires 12V takes a 12V adapter, not 9V or 15V.
For DC barrel connectors, check whether the device is center positive or center negative. Polarity must match.
The adapter must provide at least the current the device needs. A 12V 1A device can use a 12V 1A or 2A adapter, but not a 0.5A one.
A 2A adapter does not force 2 amps into the device. The device draws the current it needs. 1000 mA = 1 A.
A portable multitrack recorder with 8 XLR inputs. It records to an SD card.
8 AA batteries, or 12V DC.

cards.front: For each microphone on the F8
cards.back: Plug into the correct input. Turn on the track. Press PFL. Check and set gain. Turn on +48V phantom power if needed. Watch the meter for peaks. Listen on headphones. Record and verify.
Turning on the track on the F8 record-enables it.
Lets you focus on one channel and see the exact gain setting.
Input 1 also records to Track 5, input 2 to Track 6, input 3 to Track 7, and input 4 to Track 8.
The second track can be recorded at a lower level as a safety. If the main track clips, the quieter copy may still be usable.
With dual channel recording, tracks 5–8 hold the safety copies of inputs 1–4.
Always verify: Are the meters moving? Does it sound good in headphones? Did the recording actually save?
Video editing software. We use it to combine picture with our better-recorded audio. It is the “video side” of post-production.

1. Create or open a Library and rename clips. 2. Create a Project. 3. Import video and audio. 4. Put clips on the timeline. 5. Sync the good audio to the camera video. 6. Trim the beginning and end. 7. Add fades. 8. Check the result. 9. Export.
Video plus good audio → sync → trim → fade → QC (quality control) → export H.264 video plus WAV audio.
Where your imported media lives.
Where you watch.
Where you edit. Zoom in and out for precise edits, select clips, cut at the playhead, trim, adjust audio level, and add audio and video fades.
Import using File → Import, and choose “Leave files in place.”
Set the project to 1080p for individual movements or clips.
Disable it.
Export video as H.264, not ProRes.

cards.front: Final Cut leaves your originals alone
cards.back: Final Cut is usually not changing your original recording files. It is creating instructions: “use this part of this file, starting here, ending here, at this level.” When you export, it creates the finished file.
Keep your original files organized outside Final Cut.
YYMMDD Full Event Name, for example 260914 The Chapman Orchestra. Use the full event name for the gig folder and short names inside it.
Only add a letter after YYMMDD if that same letter is assigned in the Rec Gigs spreadsheet.
The Chapman Orchestra → TCO. Wind Symphony → WS. A studio recital of several students → studioRecital.
Raw / source files, straight from the cards.
Edit / post-production files: projects and working files.
Saved final deliverables.
Special archive or keep files.
r, e, and s describe stages and file types. They are not three backup copies of the same folder. A matching safe copy of the gig also lives on the Backups drive.
Mus128_#### means a card with a 128 GB capacity and a unique ID. IDs match the Data Volumes spreadsheet. Also Mus64_####, Mus32_####, SSDs, and so on.
Copy everything from the capture media to the Post drive and to the Backups drive, using the same gig structure on both. A hard drive can fail at any time, so one copy is not enough.
Each card or SSD gets its own From … folder inside the r folder, on both drives. Example: From Mus128_1842.
Experienced engineers may copy selectively, but only when they truly know what they are doing. For beginners, copy the whole card.
“Post Drive” and “Work Drive” may be used synonymously. In current instructions, prefer “Post Drive.”
Delete only when you can prove the source exists safely in all three places: the original card or SSD, the Post drive, and the Backups drive.
1. The approximate GB must match. 2. The last 3 digits of the exact bytes must match. 3. The location must be the expected source plus the two drives.
Do not delete. Ask for help.
Only after the checks pass: Trash, then Empty Trash, then confirm the free space.
Files in the Trash still take up space. Empty the Trash.

cards.front: Only 106 GB free on a 128 GB card?
cards.back: The Trash wasn’t emptied. After it is emptied (with the card still connected), it should show about 127 GB free. Older cards lose some maximum capacity.
Before you start, check for anything left from the last gig, such as SD cards that still need cleaning or a data transfer that never got finished. Finish that first.
Text your fellow engineers before your call time. Don’t leave them wondering.
For recording work, on time usually means ready to work at the scheduled time, not walking in at that time.
If a level is genuinely wrong, that’s a conversation with Borecki, not a knob you turn.
Hold it for about 2 seconds to turn it on or off. A quick tap does nothing, in either direction.
All 8 channels should show a red light underneath. If one isn’t lit, press that channel’s button.
Headphones on. Check both the F8 and the H6 and confirm a clean signal on both, not the same signal doubled.
Start 3 minutes before the downbeat. Confirm every recorder is actually rolling: numbers moving, not just a button pressed.
Default: leave everything recording straight through. If something is genuinely at risk, stop all recording devices together, fix it, and restart all of them together, immediately.
Use the STOP button, not the red record button. The F8 power switch needs the same 2-second hold to turn off.
Knock first. If a performer is inside, ask before touching anything, and offer to turn on the TV and show where the volume is.
Ask about changes to the program or an encore. When doors open, switch the Hallway TV from Signage to Camera and turn Hallway Audio on. At end of show, back to Signage with audio off.
Read the labels on the drives. The numbers roll forward over time, so don’t assume.
If either drive has less than 1 TB free, text Borecki. An actual text.
Create all of the destination folders on both drives first. Then copy each card into a From … folder inside both r folders.
Triple Triple Check, then get Borecki to look over the transferred files. Move to Trash, Empty Trash, then Get Info (⌘I) on the card. Free space should be close to its full size.
A doubling or halving of the light reaching the sensor. Every exposure control is measured in stops, so “give me a stop more” works on any camera.
One step along the f-number scale: 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11. F4.0 to F5.6 is one stop less light.
Double or halve the time. 1/60 to 1/30 is one stop more light.
6 dB, not 3 dB. 3 dB to 9 dB is one stop more.
Double it. ISO 400 to 800 is one stop more. ISO 400 to 1600 is two stops.

cards.front: dB and ISO aren’t a conversion
cards.back: A camera at 0 dB is at its own base sensitivity, which differs by body. 3 dB and ISO 400 are house numbers for particular cameras. What transfers is the stop: +6 dB and ISO ×2 are the same light on any camera.
It changes the color cast, not how much light hits the sensor.
How much of the scene, near to far, looks acceptably sharp.
A smaller opening (higher f-number) gives more depth of field and a darker picture. A wider opening (lower f-number) gives a shallower depth of field and more light.
Brightness has to come from somewhere: more gain costs noise, and a slower shutter costs motion blur.
F4.0 at 1/60 and F5.6 at 1/30 are about equally bright, but the second has more depth of field and more motion blur.
Aperture: depth of field. Shutter speed: motion blur. ISO or gain: noise. Once the iris is wide open, brightness has to come from the shutter or from gain.
F4.0 · 3 dB (ISO 400 on the GH5) · 1/60 · 3200 K · autofocus. Set it at the start and again before the camera goes back in the cabinet.
Reading your settings aloud on camera, so each clip records which values it used.
Pull the SD card, open the file on a computer, and confirm it plays and has audio before you shoot the rest.

cards.front: Change one thing at a time
cards.back: Keep the framing identical and change only one setting per comparison, or you can’t tell what caused the difference.
Check it’s seated and the write-protect slider is up. Do not reformat. Find a different card or ask.
Reduces the light reaching the sensor without changing the color.
In bright light it lets you keep a wide aperture (shallow depth of field) and your chosen shutter speed without overexposing. It does not help in a dark hall.
Each stop halves the light. A 3-stop ND lets through 1/8 of the light.
Measured in millimeters. A shorter focal length gives a wider view. A longer one is more zoomed in.
Zooming in lengthens the focal length and narrows the field of view. Zooming out widens it, which helps when you can’t move back.
How far from the camera the sharpest thing is. In manual focus it stays where you left it, so recheck when the subject moves.
Audio over IP: multichannel digital audio over a network. One Ethernet cable instead of a thick analog snake.
Transmit and receive.
Licensed software. Any DAW (Logic, Ableton, Reaper) can use it, and it appears as an audio interface in the DAW’s I/O.
It creates the subscription between transmit and receive channels, like a virtual patch bay across the network.
DAW I/O is where you choose the audio interface. Dante Controller chooses where network audio goes.
Set the transmitting DAW’s output device to Dante Virtual Soundcard.
Set the DAW’s input to Dante Virtual Soundcard, make a track with input Dante channels 1–2, and enable input monitoring.
Route transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 1 and transmit ch. 2 to receive ch. 2. Green squares mean connected.
The track is probably mono instead of stereo, or only one Dante channel got routed.
Note the Local Hostname (the iMac number) in System Settings > General > Sharing, then type it into the Filter Transmitters and Filter Receivers boxes.
Made in Audio MIDI Setup. It combines Dante Virtual Soundcard with your local headphones so the sending computer can hear itself while still sending. Set the DAW’s output to it.
In a Multi-Output Device, channel numbering follows the order you check the boxes. Check Dante Virtual Soundcard before the local interface.
Many senders into one receiving computer, which acts as the mixer. Each sender lands on its own track.
Transmitter 1 to receive 1–2, transmitter 2 to 3–4, transmitter 3 to 5–6. Every source needs its own receive pair.
Routing a second source to a channel pair already in use silently overrides the first. It doesn’t mix them.
Check the routing squares are green. Then check the transmitting DAW’s output and the receiving DAW’s input are both DVS, input monitoring is on, and the headphones are the selected output.
A network-wide problem. A master clock source needs to be set and active. Flag it to your instructor if you can’t resolve it.
The INST computer feeds the room’s main speakers. Breaking that route cuts sound for the whole room, including other classes.
DAW outputs 1–8, DVS transmit 1–8, the Dante network, Dante Controller subscribes TX to RX, the X32 Dante card receives 1–8, and they land on X32 faders 1–8.
Source, DAW, DVS, network, DVS, DAW, output.
Male has the pins (or the plug part that goes in); female has the holes (or the socket). Cables mate male to female.
Microphones have male XLR, so the cable’s female end goes onto the mic. The male end goes into the mixer or interface, whose inputs are female.

cards.front: Name a cable by its ends
cards.back: Say the connector and gender at each end: “XLR female to ¼-inch TRS.” Color, length, and nicknames don’t say which cable you mean.
Full-size is the standard plug. Mini and micro are smaller, in that order, and are common on cameras and other small devices. Match the cable to the port on each end.
SDI video travels on a cable with BNC connectors: round, with a twist-lock collar.
One stereo 3.5 mm plug splits into two RCA plugs: one for the left channel, one for the right.
